Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How should I answer the question about my motivation for applying for this software engineering position during an interview?
Answer: In the interview process, we are trying to determine how likely it is that a candidate will perform well in the future. Really we care about 2 things: their skillset and their accomplishments. If a candidate can demonstrate they have the required skillset and that they have achieved a lot, then this is evidence that they will perform well. A candidate that doesn’t have the skills, or that is highly skilled but hasn’t achieved what could be expected of them, doesn’t present evidence that they can do well in the future, regardless of how motivated they are. Specifically: an organization that would hire somebody because they are highly motivated but can’t pass a technical or a behavioral interview, and would reject a candidate that has excellent technical scores and a brilliant track record but doesn’t impress their interviewer with their motivation, is a circus I wouldn’t want to be a clown at. back to the question, I would respond with something vague and non committal that checks the box and move on.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the responsibilities and differences between a senior staff vs. a principal software engineer?
Answer: Those differences are fairly arbitrary and company specific. When I was at Google, L7 and L8 represented around 3% and 1% of engineer headcount respectively. L7 were senior staff engineers and senior managers, and L8 were principal engineers and directors. Companies can move that cursor any way they want, and decide where the cliff is. In my current company the staff, senior staff and principal represent 5%, 0.5% and 0.05% of all ICs. By the way, this doesn’t have to correspond to how managers are ranked and titled. I think there are 2 ways to look at senior staff vs staff / principal vs senior staff. One is: they are manifestly working on things which are one level of magnitude harder than what staff engineers / senior staff engineers are working on. By the way, identifying what one should be working on is a key part of the staff+ IC role. I said harder and not more impact intentionally. Working on low hanging fruits and unlocking lots of revenue is not how one is promoted, although that will translate into great performance evaluation, bonuses and other rewards. Difficulty of a problem is a key aspect there. Back to figuring out what should a staff+ IC work on: discovering what is the key problem an organization should tackle, when that’s not obvious to anyone, is a key part of the difficulty. At Google, principal engineers would be behind paradigm shifts that could affect an entire org. They could be like: hey, thousands of youses, instead of working like this, you should all be doing that, and drive a project that will make that seismic shift a reality. There’s a technical aspect to this (if you’re going to make thousands of people change the way they approach a problem you better be right) but there’s also a huge organizational challenge - you need to build alignment with other teams, with other organizations, which means interfacing with other super senior ICs, with execs, etc. But back to the difference between senior staff and principal, a senior staff would work on something obviously too big for one staff, an a principal would work on something obviously too big for one senior staff. A second way to look at this is organizationally. A principal engineer is usually paired with a director, not formally but typically the ratio of principal eng to director is around 1, so the principal does to an org what the director can’t and goes deep into problems rather than go wide or across. As such a principal is expected to know everything about the problem space of a ~100 people organization (at least that’s my experience). Using the same analogy, the senior staff is the peer of a senior manager, and is supposed to know beyond what’s just in front of them but don’t have to be familiar with every nook and cranny of a large organization.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some reasons why you left Accenture or Deloitte after being there for one year or more? What were your plans when you left them, and what do you do now?
Answer: Deloitte was my first job after school. I left it about a year later and the triggering factor was reading the book, The Power of Corporate Kinetics which had been written by 2 partners and distributed to the consulting staff. The TL;DR of that book is that companies can become very performant if they adopt a certain number of best practices. Not super surprising from a consulting firm. What caused me to leave was that I was seeing some of these recommendations in action in other (non-consulting) companies I interacted with, but none of them at Deloitte. I realized we were in the business of getting paid to go tell clients, do as I say not as I do. That didn’t sit well with me. Another factor that was bothering me was that my cohort of junior consultants had a general disdain for deontology and would just do whatever it takes to be promoted, putting their self interest above that of their clients, their coworkers, the firm and sometimes the law. I didn’t want to become like that. I left over 20 years ago and I’ve done a number of things since then. Even though I was a business grad, eventually I pivoted to be a software engineer in the tech industry.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do you agree with a major Silicon Valley founder who said “Every Democrat outside the Beltway knows [Biden]'ll lose”? Why or why not?
Answer: All the pundits expected a Hillary victory in 2016. Countless people had written Trump off. Turns out predicting the future is harder than it seems. In 2022/2023, dozens of tech CEOs justified rounds of layoffs with the same excuse: unpredictable macroeconomic headwinds - when this is literally their job to adjust to conjoncture. So while I don’t take predictions from anyone for absolute truth, I would trust the confidence of a “silicon valley founder” least of all.
